r: The party-list system is not exclusively for sectoral parties. National and regional parties need not represent the ‘marginalized and underrepresented’ or organize along sectoral lines. The Ang Bagong Bayani and BANAT guidelines were abandoned and six new parameters laid down.
f: COMELEC disqualified 52 party-list groups for 2013 for failing to represent marginalized sectors under the old guidelines.
h: All petitions remanded to COMELEC to apply the new parameters (COMELEC itself committed no grave abuse since it followed the old rulings).
x: The 2024 midterm (Garcia’s proposals) turns on this: any law or rule limiting the party-list to the marginalized, or requiring nominees to belong to a sector, must be squared with Atong Paglaum and with what Congress may provide ‘by law’ (Albano).
test: Parameters: (1) national, regional and sectoral parties may participate; (2) national and regional parties need not be sectoral or represent the marginalized; (3) political parties may participate through sectoral wings; (4) sectoral parties may be marginalized and underrepresented or lacking well-defined political constituencies; (5) nominees of sectoral parties must belong to the sector or have a track record of advocacy; (6) disqualification of some nominees does not disqualify the party if it has at least one qualified nominee.
g: Gatmaytan’s book: ‘The euphoria that followed [Ang Bagong Bayani] was short-lived’; the Court relied on the framers’ 19–22 vote rejecting reserved sectoral seats and on the commas in ‘national, regional, and sectoral parties’.

r: After Atong Paglaum, a sectoral party need not prove a track record; it is enough that its principal advocacy concerns the sector. Track record is required only of nominees who do not belong to the sector. Misrepresentation must relate to a qualification to justify cancellation.
f: COMELEC cancelled a peasant group’s registration for failing to show a track record and for submitting digitally altered photos of its activities.
h: Cancellation set aside; the group was declared a winner.
x: Party-list cancellation based on requirements the law does not impose.

n: Ang Ladlad LGBT Party v. COMELEC
r: COMELEC cannot deny registration on moral or religious grounds. Citing the Bible and the Koran violates non-establishment; moral disapproval of an unpopular minority is not a legitimate state interest under equal protection. The enumeration of sectors in RA 7941 is not exclusive.
f: COMELEC refused to register an LGBT party, citing immorality and religious texts.
x: Any agency or law excluding a group from the party-list (or from public participation) on moral grounds.

r: COMELEC has jurisdiction over intra-party leadership disputes and the nomination of party-list representatives, as an incident of its power to register parties and enforce election laws.
f: Two factions of CIBAC filed rival certificates of nomination for the 2010 elections.
h: COMELEC’s recognition of the faction that proved its authority was upheld.
x: Who decides a party-list leadership fight before the nominee assumes office: COMELEC.

r: COMELEC may resolve leadership disputes within a party-list group, but once a nominee has been proclaimed, has taken the oath and has assumed office, questions about his qualifications (including expulsion from the party) belong to the HRET.
f: Ating Koop’s rival factions sought COMELEC rulings on who led the party and whether its sitting representative, Lico, had been validly expelled.
h: COMELEC could not rule on Lico’s membership in the House; the Interim Central Committee (Rimas) was the legitimate leadership under the hold-over principle.
x: Party-list representative expelled by his own party: forum is the HRET, not COMELEC.

r: COMELEC, not the HRET, has jurisdiction to cancel a party-list group’s registration, even if the group already has a seat; the action does not prescribe. Allowing a nominee to assume office without COMELEC proclamation is a serious violation of RA 7941, Sec. 13.
f: In 2013 An Waray, entitled to one seat, let its second nominee assume office in the House without a COMELEC proclamation. A petition to cancel its registration was decided years later.
h: Petition dismissed (14–1, Caguioa, J.); cancellation upheld; no violation of the right to speedy disposition (Lazaro-Javier, J., dissenting).
x: Distinguish: the group’s registration (COMELEC) from the individual member’s qualifications (HRET).

n: Coalition of Associations of Senior Citizens v. COMELEC
r: Due process (notice and hearing) is indispensable before COMELEC cancels a party-list group’s registration. A term-sharing covenant among nominees is contrary to law and public policy, but cannot be a ground for cancellation where it was never implemented.
f: Senior Citizens’ nominees agreed to share one term; COMELEC cancelled its registration without a hearing.
x: Party-list term-sharing and due process before cancellation.

r: RA 7941, Sec. 8 requires a list of at least five nominees; failure to submit it is a ground to cancel registration. The list informs voters of who stands behind the group and provides for vacancies.
f: COCOFED submitted only two nominees for the 2013 elections.
x: Nominee list requirements and voters’ right to know the nominees.

r: Deadlines for withdrawal and substitution of party-list nominees stay mandatory after the election. An en masse post-election substitution blindsides voters and violates their right to information on who the nominees are. COMELEC keeps jurisdiction until the nominee validly assumes office.
f: After the 2022 elections, all five P3PWD nominees withdrew and were replaced by a new slate led by former COMELEC Commissioner Guanzon; COMELEC approved it by minute resolution.
h: Petition granted; the COMELEC resolution was void and the TRO permanent. P3PWD could submit new nominees but not the voided substitutes.
x: Party-list ‘swap’ stories: substitution after the deadline, voters’ right to know nominees, HRET versus COMELEC jurisdiction.
w: Separate matter: in 2025 COMELEC cancelled Duterte Youth’s own registration for lack of publication, and the Supreme Court denied its TRO in September 2025. That is not part of this 2024 decision.

r: The divisor for computing party-list percentages is the total valid votes for the party-list system, including votes for groups on the ballot that are later disqualified (unless disqualified with finality and made known to voters before the election). Spoiled and invalid votes are excluded. The rule applies prospectively.
f: ARARO argued all votes cast should be in the divisor; COMELEC excluded votes for disqualified groups.

n: Aksyon Magsasaka-Partido Tinig ng Masa v. COMELEC
r: COMELEC may proclaim winning party-list groups even with some votes uncanvassed, if those votes can no longer affect the result. In the second round of seat allocation, the 2% threshold no longer applies.
f: A losing group claimed COMELEC prematurely allotted additional seats in 2013 while canvassing continued.
x: Mechanics of party-list seat allocation (BANAT formula).

r: Congress may prescribe qualifications and mechanics for party-list nominees because the system operates ‘as provided by law’, but they must satisfy equal protection and due process. The ban on nominees who lost in the immediately preceding election (RA 7941, Sec. 8) has no rational basis and is void.
f: COMELEC disqualified two party-list nominees for 2022 (a losing 2019 councilor candidate and a losing 2016 and 2019 mayoral candidate) under RA 7941, Sec. 8 and COMELEC Res. 10717.
h: The ‘lost in the immediately preceding election’ ban was declared unconstitutional (Lopez, J., January 24, 2023).
x: Use directly for any proposal to amend the party-list law (2024 midterm). Congress may legislate party-list rules, but each restriction must have a rational connection to the system’s purpose.
w: Do not confuse with ANGKLA v. COMELEC (2020), which upheld the party-list seat-allocation formula in RA 7941, Sec. 11(b). Some reviewers run the two together.

r: Residence means domicile; leasing a condominium unit for under a year does not establish a new domicile. The one-year residence requirement applies even to a newly created district. A second-placer is not proclaimed when the winner is disqualified (Labo).
f: Agapito Aquino, domiciled in Tarlac, ran in Makati’s new second district after renting a unit there for about ten months.
h: Disqualified; the second placer was not proclaimed.
x: Candidates who transfer residence to run in a new district.

r: A domicile of origin is not lost without clear proof of abandonment; a wife does not automatically lose her domicile of origin by marriage. A mistake in the COC (writing seven months) does not defeat actual residence. COMELEC keeps jurisdiction until the candidate becomes a member of the House.
f: Imelda Marcos wrote ‘seven months’ of residence in Leyte’s first district in her COC; her qualifications were challenged.
h: Qualified as a resident of Tacloban.
x: Domicile of origin, marriage, and errors in the COC.

r: An incumbent official who keeps exercising his office in the place where he was elected cannot claim to have abandoned it or to intend to remain elsewhere, so he cannot meet another place’s residency requirement. The second-placer rule is abandoned: when a winner is disqualified, the vacancy is filled by succession under the Local Government Code.
f: A sitting mayor in Maguindanao ran for and won as governor of Sultan Kudarat; his COC was cancelled for material misrepresentation on residence.
h: Cancellation upheld; the Vice-Governor succeeds. Motion for reconsideration denied with finality in August 2026.
x: Use for residency of candidates and, importantly, the new rule on who takes over when a winner is disqualified. Maquiling and Chua’s proclamation of the next-ranked candidate is no longer good law on that point.

r: ‘Unless otherwise provided by law’ in Art. VI, Sec. 8 covers only (1) a law fixing another election date, or (2) a law delegating the setting of the date to COMELEC. COMELEC cannot on its own suspend a congressional election and reset it.
f: A law creating General Santos City’s lone district took effect a month before the 2019 elections; COMELEC suspended the first district’s election and moved it six months later.
h: COMELEC’s resolution was void; the new district would apply in 2022, and the winning candidate was proclaimed.
x: Election date changes by COMELEC rather than by law.

r: Under RA 6645 as amended by RA 7166, COMELEC must call and hold a special election 60 to 90 days after a House vacancy that arises at least one year before the term ends, without waiting for a House resolution certifying the vacancy. Mandamus will not lie against the House.
f: After Rep. Edward Hagedorn died in 2023, the House did not certify the vacancy and COMELEC said it needed a House resolution; no special election was held.
h: Mandamus against the House dismissed, but COMELEC’s duty clarified (Hernando, J.; Caguioa, J., concurring and dissenting). Applied in the 2026 Antipolo special election.
x: Vacancy in Congress: who calls the special election and when.
